title: India Brands Pakistan's Terrorism 'Frankenstein Monster' in Fiery UN Rebuke
excerpt: Delivering a right of reply at the UN General Assembly's Sixth Committee, diplomat Raghoo Puri said Pakistan has lost control of the terror proxies it built — and dismissed its Masood Azhar bounty hike as eyewash.
body:
• India exercised its right of reply at the UN General Assembly's Sixth Committee in New York on October 7, responding to Pakistan's Deputy Permanent Representative Usman Jadoon. First Secretary Raghoo Puri accused Pakistan of "doublespeak" on terrorism — presenting itself as a frontline state against terror while financing and sheltering terror groups.
  • Puri said the "Frankenstein monster" of terrorism that Pakistan created and lost control of has moved from "wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan" — a reality he said was acknowledged by Pakistan's own leadership.
  • He dismissed Pakistan's increase of the bounty on Jaish-e-Mohammed chief Masood Azhar — from PKR 50 lakh to 70 lakh — as eyewash, noting Islamabad called JeM "defunct" months ago and that the media has reached Azhar while the state claims ignorance of his whereabouts.
  • What it means: the exchange sets the tone ahead of the FATF plenary in Paris (October 26–30), where Pakistan's terror-financing record will be under review — a process that has previously constrained its access to international finance.

India delivered one of its sharpest rebukes of Pakistan at the United Nations on Wednesday, telling the General Assembly's Sixth Committee — which handles legal affairs — that the "Frankenstein monster" of terrorism Islamabad engineered has returned to violently stalk its own creators. First Secretary Raghoo Puri, exercising India's right of reply, said Pakistan could not continue to "run with the hares and hunt with the hounds."

"Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim, while masking the fact that the Frankenstein's (monster) the Pakistani state has created and lost control over have moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan."

— Raghoo Puri, First Secretary, India's Permanent Mission to the UN

Puri was responding to what the Indian mission described as an unprovoked tirade against New Delhi by Pakistan's Deputy Permanent Representative Usman Jadoon during proceedings on the agenda item "Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism." He pointedly declined to name two members of Pakistan's most prominent political family whose own statements, he said, had exposed the country's duplicity.

Context & Background

Puri invoked two recent admissions from within Pakistan's political establishment. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said last month in Lahore that the threat her province of 130 million people faces "comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces," and conceded that terrorism defies classification — anyone participating in extremist violence remains a terrorist regardless of political motivation.

He also reached back to a 2018 interview by her father, former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, in the Dawn newspaper: "Militant organisations are active. Call them non-state actors; should we allow them to cross the border and kill 150 people in Mumbai?"

On Masood Azhar, the UN-listed Jaish-e-Mohammed chief and mastermind of attacks on India, Puri was blunt: Pakistan's announcement of an enhanced reward for Azhar's apprehension — raising the bounty from PKR 50 lakh to 70 lakh — was an "eyewash." "Just a few months ago, Pakistani representatives used this forum to call the Jaish-e-Mohammed a defunct organisation," he said, adding: "When the media can reach Masood Azhar and get confirmation from him about the success of Operation Sindoor, surely the Pakistani state knows his whereabouts."

Impact & Analysis

Puri's intervention wove together three strands of India's longstanding case: state sponsorship, selective memory, and narrative warfare. He recalled that the world has "not forgotten 9/11, and where its perpetrators, including Osama bin Laden, were caught" — a reference to the al-Qaeda leader found living near the Pakistan Military Academy in Abbottabad — "nor 26/11," when terrorists killed 166 people across Mumbai in 2008, "nor Pahalgam," where attackers singled out Hindu and Christian tourists by asking their religion before killing them.

"The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation; they were asked about their religion," Puri said. "It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism."

On Operation Sindoor — India's retaliatory strikes following the Pahalgam attack — Puri mocked Pakistan's victory narrative: "If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are, of course, welcome to enjoy it." When the Pakistani delegation returned to the podium with a second intervention, he cut it down: "Pakistan believes in the circular economy of words and narratives," adding that "nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government" — a reference to allegations that Pakistan's 2024 elections were rigged through falsified result forms to install Shehbaz Sharif.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the exchange lands in familiar territory: the Pahalgam attack struck at tourists, including families on holiday, and diaspora households have long followed the diplomacy around 26/11 justice. The practical stakes are financial as much as moral — a country flagged for terror financing faces higher compliance costs and constrained access to international capital, which ripples through trade and remittance corridors.

What's Next

Pakistan issued its own second right of reply through counsellor Muhammad Jawad Ajmal, accusing India of backing proxies in Afghanistan — a claim New Delhi rejects. The immediate test of Puri's arguments comes at the Financial Action Task Force plenary in Paris from October 26 to 30, where Pakistan's record on terror financing will again be under scrutiny. "The world has seen the script play earlier," Puri said, "and we are clear-eyed that this time also it is going to be no different."
